newsitem.title: USA: SEC charges Italy's Montedison with accounting fraud.
newsitem.headline: SEC charges Italy's Montedison with accounting fraud.

text.p: U.S. regulators on Thursday charged Italy's Montedison SpA with accounting fraud, alleging the conglomerate doctored financial data to hide nearly $400 million in losses and funnelled money to pay bribes to Italian politicians.
The Securities and Exchange Commission said the bribes were disguised as legitimate loans or in other outlined in the company's financial statements filed in the United States.
In a complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, the SEC also charged Montedison with violating corporate reporting regulations and other rules under U.S. securities laws.

The stock of the Milan-based conglomerate -- which operates agricultural, chemical, energy and engineering businesses -- has traded on the New York Stock Exchange since July 1987. As a result, it files annual reports and other statements with the SEC.
The SEC alleged that the scheme concealed losses of at least $398 million and hid hundreds of millions of dollars of bribes paid by the company to Italian politicians and other officials.
It charged Montedison with violating securities law "by engaging in a fraudulent scheme to materially misstate its financial condition and results of its operations" on reports filed with the agency.

Montedison said it had yet to review the complaint but noted it was based on events that were disclosed more than three years ago. It said the managers involved had left the company or been discharged.
In a statement, it said it "will continue to cooperate with the SEC and shall seek to resolve this litigation promptly," adding that no fines were warranted.
Paul Gerlach, an SEC associate director for enforcement, characterised Montedison's scheme as "a long-running fraud."
"They were using company assets to pay bribes, funnelling money to offshore entities as legitimate loans, but it was a sham," he said.
The agency could seek fines of up to $500,000 for each alleged violation, he said, adding the agency has not decided how much to seek in penalties.
The SEC alleged that from December 1988 to May 1993, numerous undocumented payments running into hundreds of millions of dollars were made by the company or its agents.

In one case, the SEC alleged Montedison arranged with a Rome developer to effect real estate deals at artificially high prices. The developer then used the money to bribe Italian politicians and other people on Montedison's behalf, the agency alleged.

Montedison's goal in the scheme, the SEC alleged, was to gain control of Enimont, a joint venture with the Italian state energy company ENI. At the time, a Milan judge had frozen ENI's and Montedison's shares in the joint venture and gave custody and voting rights to a third party, the SEC said.

The inflated real estate deals were used to disguise the bribes on the company's books from 1990 to 1992, which resulted in Montedison taking writeoffs of $126.3 million in its 1993 financial reports, the agency said.

In another scheme, Montedison fictitiously "loaned" about $272 million to a Curacao, Netherlands Antilles, company that then funnelled the money to Exilar International SA, a British Virgin Islands firm.
In the latter half of 1993, Montedison decided the loan was "uncollectible" and took a write-down of the whole amount for its 1992 fiscal year, the SEC alleged.
Montedison's U.S. shares fell 25 cents to $6.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
